title: Architect Secure AI Infrastructure and Platforms
intro: Securing the platforms AI runs on: hardening cloud, on-premises and hybrid deployments; isolating and sandboxing training and inference workloads, including code that agents write; protecting availability against resource exhaustion with throttling, quotas and scheduling; isolating accelerator capacity; and the physical and environmental security of power-dense AI data centres.
objectives: Harden AI infrastructure across ML tooling, serving, orchestration, compute and network layers, in cloud, on-premises and hybrid deployments
Choose isolation and sandboxing for training, inference and agent-generated code according to data sensitivity and trust
Protect AI infrastructure from resource exhaustion with layered rate limits, compute throttling, quotas, priorities and autoscaling limits
Isolate accelerator capacity through partitioning, dedicated and reserved capacity, memory hygiene and confidential GPU computing
Apply power, cooling, physical access and fire protection controls suited to high-density AI facilities

sections.title: Hardening cloud, on-premises and hybrid AI deployments

scenes.title: Hardening the AI stack
scenes.say: AI platforms are built from ordinary infrastructure, often deployed in a hurry: GPU clusters, notebooks, model servers and orchestration tools, many designed for researchers rather than adversaries. | This video covers hardening AI deployments in the cloud, on premises, and across both.

scenes.title: The AI infrastructure stack
scenes.say: Every layer of the AI stack needs hardening. | At the top, machine learning tooling: notebooks, experiment trackers, pipelines and dashboards, often the weakest point. | Model serving: inference servers, gateways and endpoints. | Orchestration: Kubernetes, distributed compute frameworks and job schedulers. | Compute and accelerators: hosts, GPUs, drivers and firmware. | And underneath it all, the network, identity and storage layer: virtual networks, access management, storage buckets and keys.

scenes.title: Common weaknesses

items.d: Tokens and keys left in code and output
Broad roles on clusters and buckets

scenes.say: The same weaknesses appear again and again. | Dashboards and job APIs reachable from the internet without authentication. In 2024, attackers exploited exposed clusters running Ray, a popular distributed AI framework whose job interface lacked authentication by default, to steal credentials and computing power. | Secrets left in notebooks: tokens and keys in code cells and saved output. | Unpatched drivers, inference servers and frameworks. | Datasets and model checkpoints in publicly readable storage. | Over-privileged service accounts on clusters and buckets. | And flat networks with open internet egress, where one foothold reaches everything.

scenes.title: Cloud, on-premises and hybrid
rows: One identity, private links, one policy
scenes.say: Responsibilities shift with the deployment model. | In the cloud, you harden configuration, identity and data. On premises, you harden everything, down to the hardware. In hybrid deployments, you harden both, plus the links between them. | Cloud risks centre on misconfiguration and public endpoints. On-premises risks include patching, firmware and physical security. Hybrid adds inconsistent policies and exposed connections. | So in the cloud, use organisation-wide policy guardrails and private endpoints. On premises, use hardened images and an isolated management network. And for hybrid, use one identity system, private connectivity, and one policy applied everywhere.

scenes.title: A hardening baseline
scenes.say: A practical baseline has six parts. | Start from published benchmarks, such as the CIS benchmarks for operating systems, Kubernetes and cloud platforms. | Make everything private by default: no public endpoints, no public buckets. | Use least-privilege identities, with workload identity rather than long-lived keys. | Patch the whole AI stack, including GPU drivers, inference servers and frameworks. | Harden containers: minimal images, running as non-root, signed and checked at admission. | And log and monitor the control plane, data access and GPU usage, so misuse is spotted quickly.

items: Harden every layer, from tooling to network and identity
ML tools are often exposed, unauthenticated and full of secrets
Cloud, on-premises and hybrid shift what you harden
Benchmarks, private by default, least privilege, patching, monitoring
scenes.say: To recap. | Harden every layer of the AI stack, from machine learning tools down to network, identity and storage. | Machine learning tools are often exposed, unauthenticated and full of secrets, so start there. | Cloud, on-premises and hybrid deployments shift what you have to harden. | And build on benchmarks, private-by-default networking, least privilege, patching and monitoring.

blocks.md:
### Why AI infrastructure is a soft target
AI platforms combine high-value assets (data, weights, GPU capacity) with tools built for fast experimentation: notebooks, experiment trackers, model registries, distributed compute frameworks and inference servers. Many ship with authentication off or optional, assume a trusted network, and are deployed by data scientists rather than platform engineers.

**Case: ShadowRay (2024).** Researchers reported active exploitation of internet-exposed clusters running Ray, a widely used distributed computing framework for AI. Ray’s job submission API had no authentication by default (the project’s position was that clusters should only run in trusted, isolated networks). Attackers used exposed clusters to run arbitrary code, steal cloud credentials and tokens, access data and models, and mine cryptocurrency on GPUs. The lesson: **never expose AI tooling directly to the internet**, and treat "it’s meant for a trusted network" as a requirement you must enforce.

### Hardening by layer
| Layer | Key hardening controls |
|---|---|
| **ML tooling** | Authentication and SSO on notebooks, trackers, registries and dashboards; private access only; secret scanning of notebooks and repositories; per-user environments rather than shared kernels |
| **Model serving** | Authenticated endpoints, disabled debug and admin interfaces, input size limits, patched inference servers, minimal images, network policies |
| **Orchestration** | Kubernetes RBAC with least privilege, network policies, Pod Security Standards (restricted profile), encrypted secrets, audit logging, admission control for signed images |
| **Compute and accelerators** | Hardened OS images, timely GPU driver and firmware updates, isolated baseboard management (BMC) networks, disabled unused services |
| **Network, identity and storage** | Private endpoints, segmentation, egress filtering, workload identity, no long-lived keys, encryption with managed keys, blocking public buckets by policy |

### Deployment models
- **Cloud:** use organisation-level policies (for example, service control policies or organisation constraints) to block public endpoints and buckets, restrict regions and enforce encryption; manage everything as **infrastructure as code** with policy checks; use posture management (CSPM, AI-SPM and DSPM, Module 3.4) to detect drift.
- **On-premises:** you own patching, firmware, physical security and capacity; keep management networks isolated; maintain golden images; plan GPU driver and firmware updates as part of change management.
- **Hybrid:** unify identity (federation, single sign-on), connect sites through private interconnects or encrypted tunnels, apply the same policies and monitoring in both, and make sure data residency rules are enforced wherever workloads run.

### Baseline references
CIS Benchmarks (operating systems, Kubernetes, cloud foundations), cloud providers’ security reference architectures for AI services, the NSA and CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide, and vendor security bulletins for GPU drivers and inference servers.

blocks.title: Hardening questions
blocks.md: If an AI tool is exposed to the internet, the first fix is almost always to **remove the exposure** (private networking with authentication) and check for compromise, not to add monitoring or ask users to be careful. "Designed for trusted networks" means you must provide that trusted network.

q.q: A data science team runs a distributed training cluster whose dashboard and job API are reachable from the internet, so that remote staff can use them. What is the BEST action?
o: Leave it reachable, but add a banner warning that access is for authorised staff only
Move it behind private networking with authentication, and check for signs of compromise
Change the dashboard to a non-standard port number so that scanners are less likely to find it
Ask staff to keep the dashboard address confidential and not share it outside the team
q.why: Internet-exposed AI tooling without strong authentication is actively exploited. Removing exposure and requiring authentication fixes the root cause, and checking for compromise addresses what may already have happened. Banners, unusual ports and secrecy are not controls.

sections.title: Isolation and sandboxing for training and inference

scenes.title: Walls between workloads
scenes.sub: Isolation and sandboxing for training and inference
scenes.say: AI workloads handle sensitive data, load models from outside, and increasingly run code that the model wrote itself. Isolation decides how far a compromise can spread. | This video covers isolation and sandboxing for training and inference workloads.

scenes.title: How strong is the wall?
scenes.say: Isolation comes in degrees, and stronger walls cost more. | Separate processes share the operating system and its resources, which is very little isolation. | Containers give separate file systems, but share the host’s kernel, so a kernel exploit crosses the wall. | Sandboxed containers add a user-space kernel or a lightweight virtual machine, which is much stronger for untrusted code. | Virtual machines have separate kernels, but still share hardware. | Dedicated hosts or clusters separate the hardware itself. | And air-gapped environments have no network path at all, for the most sensitive work.

scenes.title: An isolated training environment
scenes.say: Here is an isolated training environment for sensitive data. The training cluster sits inside its own enclave: a separate account or project and network. | Engineers reach it only through secure, authenticated access, such as a bastion or privileged access workstation, never directly from the internet. | Training data comes from an approved, pinned mirror over a private endpoint. | Direct internet egress is blocked, so stolen data or weights can’t simply be sent out, and nothing can be downloaded without review. | And the only way out for results is the model registry, which accepts signed artefacts.

scenes.title: Sandboxing code that agents run
scenes.say: When an agent writes and runs code, that code is untrusted, whoever asked for it. Sandbox it. | Make sandboxes ephemeral: created fresh for each task and destroyed afterwards. | Use strong isolation, such as micro-virtual machines or sandboxed container runtimes, not plain containers. | Give no network access by default, and allow-list only the destinations a task genuinely needs. | Limit CPU, memory, disk and running time, so a loop or a fork bomb can’t exhaust the host. | Keep secrets out of the sandbox, injecting narrowly scoped tokens only when essential. | And treat the files and results that come out as untrusted input.

scenes.title: Isolating tenants at inference
scenes.say: Multi-tenant inference needs a deliberate isolation choice. | A shared model server separates tenants logically, request by request. Per-tenant deployments run separate instances. Confidential computing adds hardware-enforced isolation. | If logical separation fails, data can leak between tenants, for example through shared caches. Separate instances contain a failure to one tenant, and confidential computing adds attestation that the protection is in place. | Shared servers suit low-risk, high-scale services. Per-tenant deployments suit regulated tenants. And confidential computing suits highly sensitive data on infrastructure you don’t control.

items: Choose wall strength by sensitivity and trust
Training enclaves: secure access, private data, no egress, signed outputs
Sandbox agent code: ephemeral, isolated, offline, limited, no secrets
Pick inference isolation per tenant risk; never share caches across tenants
scenes.say: To recap. | Choose the strength of isolation according to data sensitivity and how much you trust the code. | Put sensitive training in an enclave with secure access, private data, no internet egress and signed outputs. | Sandbox agent-generated code: ephemeral, strongly isolated, offline by default, resource-limited and free of secrets. | And choose inference isolation according to each tenant’s risk, never sharing caches between tenants.

blocks.md:
### Choosing isolation
| Workload | Typical risk | Suitable isolation |
|---|---|---|
| Experiments on public or synthetic data | Low | Shared clusters with namespaces, quotas and network policies |
| Training on confidential or personal data | High | Dedicated account or project, segmented network, no internet egress, private endpoints, dedicated nodes |
| Training on highly sensitive or regulated data | Very high | Dedicated clusters or hosts, confidential computing, or air-gapped environments |
| Loading third-party models | Untrusted artefacts | Scan and convert in a sandbox before use (Modules 3.6 and 3.7) |
| Agent-generated code | Untrusted code | Ephemeral micro-VM or sandboxed runtime, offline by default |
| Multi-tenant inference | Cross-tenant leakage | Per-tenant instances or namespaces for sensitive tenants; per-tenant caches; confidential computing where required |

### Training environments
- **Separate accounts or projects** per sensitivity level, with their own identities and keys.
- **No direct internet egress**; package and model downloads come through approved, scanned internal mirrors.
- **Private endpoints** to storage and registries; data pinned by hash (Module 3.7).
- **Secure administrative access** through bastions or privileged access workstations, with MFA and session recording.
- **Controlled export:** results leave only through the model registry, signed and approved (Modules 3.5 and 3.6).

### Code execution sandboxes
Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability lets code escape. For untrusted code, use **micro-VMs** (such as Firecracker) or **sandboxed runtimes** (such as gVisor or Kata Containers), and add: ephemeral instances; no network or an egress allow-list; seccomp profiles and read-only file systems; CPU, memory, disk and time limits; no credentials; and inspection of outputs. Many AI code interpreters are built this way.

### Inference isolation and shared caches
Inference servers reuse computation between requests, for example through **prompt or key-value caches**. Researchers auditing commercial LLM APIs in 2025 found that some providers shared prompt caches across users, which created timing side channels that could reveal whether another user had sent a similar prompt. Keep caches **per tenant or per organisation** for sensitive workloads, and ask providers how caching is scoped. Also isolate tenants’ logs, fine-tunes, adapters and retrieval indexes.

### Notebooks and developer environments
Give each user their own environment rather than shared kernels, restrict their network access, keep secrets in a vault rather than in notebooks, and scan notebooks and repositories for leaked credentials.

blocks.title: Isolation questions
blocks.md: Match isolation to **trust in the code** and **sensitivity of the data**. Plain containers are not a strong boundary for untrusted code; micro-VMs, sandboxed runtimes, VMs or dedicated hardware are. For sensitive training, the hallmarks are **no internet egress, private data access and controlled export**.

blocks.title: Match the workload to its isolation
pairs: Python code written by an agent
Dedicated enclave with no internet egress
Shared cluster with quotas and network policies
A regulated tenant on a shared inference service
Scan and convert it in a sandbox first

q.q: An agent writes and runs Python code to analyse spreadsheets that users upload. Where should that code run?
o: In the agent’s own application container, which already has access to the files
In an ephemeral, strongly isolated sandbox with no network, resource limits and no secrets
On the user’s own laptop, so that any damage is limited to that one device
In a long-lived container shared by every user’s analysis jobs, so results come back quickly
q.why: Model-generated code is untrusted. An ephemeral, strongly isolated sandbox without network access, secrets or unlimited resources contains anything it does. The application container holds broader access, users’ devices aren’t controlled, and shared long-lived containers let one job affect others.

blocks.title: Don’t let one job starve the rest

scenes.title: Don’t let one job starve the rest
scenes.sub: Throttling, quotas, scheduling and autoscaling limits
scenes.say: GPU capacity is scarce and expensive. One runaway training job, a flood of inference requests or a looping agent can starve everything else, by accident or by design. | This video covers infrastructure-level controls against resource exhaustion: throttling, quotas, scheduling and autoscaling limits.

scenes.title: How AI infrastructure gets exhausted

items.d: One team or tenant hogs GPUs

scenes.say: Resources run out in six common ways. | Runaway jobs: bugs, infinite loops and oversized batches. | Inference floods, from genuine traffic spikes or deliberate attacks. | Agent loops: endless tool calls and retries. | Noisy neighbours: one team or tenant taking all the GPUs. | Memory exhaustion from very long contexts or ever-growing caches. | And hijacked compute: attackers who gain access to a cluster often use its GPUs for cryptocurrency mining.

scenes.title: Layers of throttling
scenes.say: Throttling works best in layers, each catching what the last one misses. Requests and jobs arrive from users, applications and agents. | The gateway applies rate limits that count tokens as well as requests, per identity. | An admission queue holds work when capacity is short, admits it by priority, and sheds the least important work first. | The scheduler enforces quotas for each team or tenant, and lets critical workloads preempt experiments. | On the GPU nodes themselves, limits on memory, concurrency and running time stop any one job from taking everything. | And autoscaling adds capacity, but only up to a set maximum, with budget alerts, so an attack can’t scale costs without limit.

scenes.title: Three kinds of control
scenes.say: Three kinds of control work together. | Rate limiting works on requests and tokens. Compute throttling works on GPU, memory and time. Quotas and priorities work on teams and workloads. | Rate limiting protects against floods and abuse. Compute throttling protects against runaway jobs and loops. Quotas and priorities stop critical work from being starved. | For example: a limit on tokens per minute for each key; caps on each job’s running time and memory; and a rule that production inference always outranks experiments.

scenes.title: Detect and respond
scenes.say: Limits need monitoring and a response. | Watch GPU utilisation, queue depth and latency, with baselines for each service. | Alert on unusual jobs, such as unknown workloads running at full load for hours, a classic sign of cryptomining. | Raise budget and capacity alerts before limits are reached, not after. | Stop jobs that break their limits automatically, keeping a record for investigation. | And under pressure, shed low-priority load first, so the most important services keep running.

items: Runaway jobs, floods, loops, neighbours and hijacking exhaust capacity
Layer gateway, queue, scheduler, node and autoscaling limits
Rate limits, compute throttling and quotas do different jobs
Monitor, alert, stop and shed load to protect critical services
scenes.say: To recap. | Runaway jobs, floods, agent loops, noisy neighbours and hijacked compute can all exhaust AI infrastructure. | Layer controls at the gateway, the admission queue, the scheduler, the nodes and autoscaling. | Rate limits, compute throttling and quotas do different jobs, so use all three. | And monitor, alert, stop runaway work and shed low-priority load to protect critical services.

blocks.md:
### Controls by layer
| Layer | Controls |
|---|---|
| **Edge and gateway** | DDoS protection; authentication; rate limits on requests **and tokens** per key, user and tenant; input and output token caps (Module 3.6) |
| **Admission and queueing** | Bounded queues; priority classes; load shedding of low-priority work; timeouts while queued |
| **Scheduling** | Per-team or per-tenant GPU quotas; fair-share scheduling; preemption so critical workloads can displace experiments; placement rules that keep production on reserved nodes |
| **Nodes and runtimes** | CPU, memory and GPU limits per workload; job time limits; maximum context length and concurrent sequences on inference servers, to bound memory used by key-value caches |
| **Autoscaling** | Maximum replica counts; scale-out rate limits; budget alerts and hard caps; separate budgets for experimentation |
| **Agents** | Step, tool-call, time and cost budgets per task, with loop detection (Module 4.6) |

In Kubernetes, these map to features such as **resource requests and limits**, **ResourceQuotas** and **LimitRanges** per namespace, **PriorityClasses** with preemption, job deadlines, and batch schedulers that manage GPU quotas and fair sharing. Traditional HPC schedulers provide similar controls.

### Detecting exhaustion and abuse
- Baseline GPU utilisation, memory, queue depth, latency and error rates per service.
- Alert on unknown or unapproved workloads, sustained full GPU load outside schedules, new outbound connections from training nodes, and sudden cost spikes. Cryptomining after a cluster compromise is common (as in the ShadowRay campaign, Section 1).
- Correlate infrastructure signals with gateway logs to separate genuine demand from abuse (Module 5.3).

### Responding
Throttle or block offending identities, kill runaway jobs, shed low-priority load, fail over to reserved capacity or fallback models (Module 3.6), and investigate whether exhaustion was accidental or malicious. Module 6.1 covers availability attacks such as compute and token exhaustion, and Module 4.4 covers load and stress testing to find limits before attackers do.

blocks.title: Exhaustion questions
blocks.md: For shared clusters, the best answers combine **quotas** (fair shares), **priorities with preemption** (critical work wins) and **limits** (time, memory, maximum scale). Simply buying more GPUs, or asking teams to be careful, doesn’t prevent a single job or attacker from consuming everything.

q.q: A shared GPU cluster runs a production inference service and data scientists’ experiments. A buggy experiment used every GPU for six hours, and inference degraded. What is the BEST preventive control?
o: Ask data scientists to check their experiments more carefully before submitting them
Per-team quotas, priorities that let production preempt experiments, and job time limits
Buy enough additional GPUs that the cluster can no longer run out of capacity
Run experiments only overnight, when inference traffic is usually much lower
q.why: Quotas cap each team’s share, preemption guarantees production capacity, and time limits stop runaway jobs. More hardware can be consumed just the same, scheduling by time of day doesn’t stop a runaway job, and carefulness isn’t a control.

scenes.title: Whose GPU is it anyway?
scenes.say: Accelerators are the heart of AI infrastructure, and they are often shared: between teams, between tenants, and between customers of a cloud provider. | This video covers isolated accelerator capacity: why sharing GPUs creates risk, and the options for keeping critical and sensitive workloads apart.

scenes.title: Ways to share a GPU
scenes.say: There are three broad ways to share an accelerator. | Time-slicing lets workloads take turns on the same GPU, sharing its memory, which is weak isolation. Hardware partitioning, such as multi-instance GPU technology, splits one GPU into slices with their own memory and compute. Dedicated GPUs give full isolation. | With time-slicing, performance is unpredictable. Hardware partitions give each slice predictable performance, and dedicated GPUs are the most predictable of all. | So use time-slicing only for trusted, low-priority work, hardware partitions for mixed workloads and tenants, and dedicated GPUs for sensitive or critical work.

scenes.title: Risks of shared accelerators

items.d: A shared host is a shared target

scenes.say: Sharing accelerators brings six risks. | Leftover data: if GPU memory isn’t cleared between jobs, the next workload may read what the last one left behind. In 2024, researchers showed this on several vendors’ GPUs, recovering parts of another process’s language model output. | Side channels, such as timing, cache behaviour and power use, which can leak information across workloads. | Contention, where noisy neighbours starve critical work. | Flaws in drivers and firmware, which make a shared host a shared target. | Capacity loss, through shortages or cheap instances that the provider reclaims at short notice. | And concentration, where all capacity depends on one provider or one region.

scenes.title: Placing workloads on accelerators
scenes.say: Sensitivity and availability together decide where a workload should run. | Highly sensitive and critical: dedicated GPUs with reserved capacity. | Highly sensitive but best-effort: dedicated GPUs, or confidential GPU computing on shared infrastructure. | Low sensitivity but critical, such as a public service: reserved capacity, partitioned if shared. | And low sensitivity, best-effort work, such as most experiments: a shared pool with quotas.

scenes.title: Controls for accelerator capacity
scenes.say: Six controls cover most of this risk. | Reserve capacity for critical services, through reservations or committed capacity, rather than competing for on-demand GPUs in a shortage. | Use hardware partitions, not time-slicing, when tenants or sensitivity levels share a GPU. | Clear accelerator memory between jobs, by scrubbing or resetting devices. | Patch drivers and firmware promptly, and keep management interfaces isolated. | Use confidential GPU computing, with attestation, for sensitive work on shared infrastructure. | And plan for scarcity, with multiple regions or providers and fallback models.

items: Time-slicing shares memory; partitions and dedicated GPUs isolate
Shared accelerators risk leftover data, side channels and contention
Place workloads by sensitivity and availability need
Reserve, partition, scrub, patch, attest, and plan for scarcity
scenes.say: To recap. | Time-slicing shares memory, while hardware partitions and dedicated GPUs provide real isolation. | Shared accelerators risk leftover data, side channels, contention and shared vulnerabilities. | Place each workload according to its data sensitivity and availability need. | And reserve critical capacity, partition shared GPUs, clear memory, patch, use attestation for sensitive work, and plan for scarcity.

blocks.md:
### Sharing models for accelerators
| Approach | How it works | Isolation | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Time-slicing** | Workloads take turns on the whole GPU | Weak: shared memory and caches | Simple; unpredictable performance; for trusted workloads only |
| **Multi-process sharing** | Several processes run concurrently on one GPU | Weak to moderate | Better utilisation; limited fault and memory isolation |
| **Hardware partitioning** (such as NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU) | One GPU is split into up to seven instances, each with dedicated memory, cache and compute | Strong, enforced in hardware | Predictable performance; supported on recent data-centre GPUs |
| **Virtual GPUs** | A hypervisor presents GPU slices to virtual machines | Moderate to strong, depending on configuration | Common in virtual desktop and some cloud offerings |
| **Dedicated GPUs or hosts** | One workload or tenant per device or server | Full | Highest cost; required for the most sensitive or critical work |

### Real-world risk: leftover GPU memory
In January 2024, researchers disclosed **LeftoverLocals**, a vulnerability on GPUs from several vendors that let one process read data left in GPU local memory by another. They demonstrated recovering fragments of another user’s language model responses. Vendors released fixes, but the lesson is general: **clear accelerator memory between workloads**, and don’t rely on sharing for isolation between tenants or sensitivity levels.

### Designing isolated capacity
- **Dedicated pools** for sensitive or regulated training, kept apart through separate clusters or node pools, with scheduler rules (labels, taints and tolerations) so other workloads can’t land on them.
- **Reserved capacity** for production inference and other critical services; avoid preemptible or spot capacity for anything that must stay up.
- **Hardware partitioning** for multi-tenant serving on shared GPUs, combined with per-tenant caches (Section 2).
- **Confidential GPU computing** on recent data-centre GPUs encrypts CPU–GPU transfers and protects GPU memory, with attestation before keys or data are released (Module 2.5).
- **Hygiene:** reset or scrub GPUs between jobs; keep drivers, firmware and container toolkits patched (vendors publish regular security bulletins); isolate baseboard management controllers on a separate management network.
- **Resilience and sovereignty:** advanced accelerators can be scarce and subject to export controls, so plan multi-region or multi-provider capacity, keep fallback models ready (Module 3.6), and check where capacity is located when data residency matters.

blocks.title: Accelerator questions
blocks.md: When tenants or sensitivity levels share GPUs, look for **hardware partitioning** and **memory clearing**, or **dedicated capacity** for the most sensitive and critical work. Time-slicing is about utilisation, not isolation. For critical services, **reserved capacity** beats competing for on-demand GPUs.

q.q: A platform team wants three internal tenants with different data sensitivity to share one multi-GPU server. Which approach BEST balances isolation and utilisation?
o: Time-slice every GPU across all three tenants, which gives the best overall utilisation of the server
Hardware-isolated GPU partitions per tenant, memory clearing, and dedicated GPUs where needed
Let the tenants schedule their own jobs, and rely on them to agree among themselves
Run all three tenants’ jobs inside one shared container, so management stays simple
q.why: Hardware partitions give each tenant separate memory and compute, memory clearing prevents leftover data, and dedicated GPUs remain available where sensitivity demands them. Time-slicing shares memory, self-scheduling isn’t a control, and a shared container provides no isolation.

sections.title: Physical and environmental security for AI data centres

scenes.title: Power, cooling and locks
scenes.sub: Physical and environmental security for AI data centres
scenes.say: AI hardware is dense, hot and power-hungry, and it concentrates enormous value in a few racks. Physical and environmental security has to keep up. | This video covers power, cooling, rack security and fire protection for AI data centres.

scenes.title: Power per rack has exploded
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative power draw per rack, in kilowatts
scenes.say: Power density has exploded. In this illustrative chart, a typical enterprise rack draws under ten kilowatts, while an air-cooled GPU rack draws several times that. | Current liquid-cooled AI racks can exceed a hundred kilowatts each, and next-generation designs go higher still. | That changes everything downstream: power distribution, cooling, floor loading and fire risk. A data hall designed for ordinary servers usually can’t simply take AI racks.

scenes.title: Power and cooling

items.d: Capacity to survive a lost unit

scenes.say: Power and cooling need six things. | Redundant power: N plus one or fully duplicated paths, with uninterruptible power supplies and generators. | Liquid cooling, either direct to the chip or by immersion, because air alone can’t remove the heat from dense AI racks. | Leak detection, with sensors in and under racks, because liquid now runs right next to the electronics. | Thermal monitoring of inlet temperatures and hotspots. | Headroom, so the site can lose a cooling unit or power path and keep running. | And secure supply: grid capacity, which is now a real constraint for AI sites, and fuel contracts for generators.

scenes.title: Rack and facility security

items.d: GPUs and drives tracked end to end

scenes.say: Physical access control works in layers too. | Zones nest from the site perimeter, through the building and the data hall, down to the cage and the individual rack. | Entry to sensitive zones needs more than one factor, such as a badge plus a biometric, with mantraps to stop tailgating. | Racks holding AI hardware are locked electronically, with every opening logged. | Surveillance covers the space, and visitors are always escorted. | GPUs and drives are high-value and data-bearing, so track their chain of custody from delivery to destruction. | And tamper detection, such as door sensors and seals, shows when a rack has been opened.

scenes.title: Fire detection and suppression
scenes.say: Fire protection combines detection and suppression. | Aspirating systems sample the air continuously for smoke particles. Gas systems flood the room with a clean agent or inert gas. Water-based systems, such as pre-action sprinklers or water mist, release water only when needed. | Early detection gives warning long before visible smoke. Gas leaves no residue on equipment. Water-based systems are effective and often required by building codes. | But detection needs tuning to avoid false alarms. Gas needs well-sealed rooms and procedures to keep people safe. And water risks damaging the very equipment it protects.

items: AI racks draw many times more power, and need liquid cooling
Redundant power, leak detection, thermal headroom
Layered access, audited racks, chain of custody for hardware
Early detection plus suppression suited to the equipment
scenes.say: To recap. | AI racks draw many times the power of ordinary servers, and usually need liquid cooling. | Provide redundant power, leak detection and thermal headroom. | Layer physical access down to audited racks, and track hardware from delivery to destruction. | And pair very early fire detection with suppression suited to the equipment and the people in the space.

blocks.md:
### Power
- **Redundancy levels:** *N* (just enough capacity), *N+1* (one spare component), *2N* (fully duplicated systems and paths) and *2N+1*. Critical AI services usually need at least N+1, and often 2N, for power distribution.
- **UPS and generators:** uninterruptible power supplies bridge the gap until generators start; plan generator fuel for an extended outage, with supply contracts. Lithium-ion UPS batteries are compact, but need fire risk management (thermal runaway).
- **Distribution:** AI racks need higher-capacity power distribution and busways; check breaker coordination and power quality monitoring.
- **Grid capacity** is now a major constraint for new AI sites; understand utility commitments and on-site generation plans.

### Cooling
- **Air cooling** struggles beyond a few tens of kilowatts per rack; hot and cold aisle containment helps.
- **Direct-to-chip liquid cooling** pipes coolant to cold plates on processors; **immersion cooling** submerges hardware in dielectric fluid. Both bring new risks: leaks, pump and coolant distribution unit failures, and, for some immersion fluids, flammability and handling requirements.
- Follow the ASHRAE thermal guidelines for equipment environments, monitor inlet temperatures, and keep redundant pumps and chillers.
- **Floor loading:** AI racks are heavy, often well over a tonne, so check structural limits.

### Physical security
ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A includes physical controls such as security perimeters, physical entry controls, monitoring, protection against environmental threats, equipment siting, supporting utilities, cabling security, equipment maintenance and secure disposal. For AI facilities, emphasise:
- **Layered zones** with multi-factor entry, mantraps and anti-tailgating, and an access review process.
- **Locked, monitored racks and cages**, with audit trails of every opening.
- **CCTV with retention**, visitor escort, and logging of contractor access.
- **Chain of custody** for accelerators and storage from delivery to decommissioning; sanitise or destroy media before it leaves (Module 3.4).
- **Tamper evidence** on racks and hardware.

### Fire protection
- **Very early warning aspirating smoke detection** samples air through pipes and can detect incipient fires.
- **Gaseous suppression** uses clean agents or inert gases that leave no residue; it needs sealed rooms, safety interlocks and evacuation procedures, and some agents are being phased down for environmental reasons.
- **Pre-action sprinklers** keep pipes dry until two independent signals occur, reducing accidental discharge; **water mist** uses less water.
- Relevant standards include NFPA 75 (protection of IT equipment) and NFPA 2001 (clean agent systems).

### Site and resilience standards
**ANSI/TIA-942** rates data centre infrastructure from rating 1 to 4; the **Uptime Institute** tiers range from Tier I (basic capacity) through Tier III (concurrently maintainable, so any component can be maintained without downtime) to Tier IV (fault tolerant). **EN 50600** is the European data centre standard. When AI runs in third-party facilities, verify these controls through certifications and audit reports (Module 2.5).

### Environmental monitoring
Monitor temperature, humidity, water and leaks, smoke, power quality and door status, with alerts to staffed operations, and test responses regularly.

blocks.title: Physical security questions
blocks.md: Remember that AI changes the **scale** of familiar physical risks: far higher power and heat per rack, liquid near electronics, heavier racks, and very valuable hardware. Good answers address **capacity and redundancy** first when new AI hardware is installed, and **layered access with auditing** for protecting it.

blocks.title: Facility vocabulary
cards: One spare component beyond what the load needs.
Two complete, independent systems, either able to carry the full load.
Two interlocked doors that admit one person at a time, stopping tailgating.
Pipes stay dry until two independent signals occur, reducing accidental discharge.
Continuously samples air for smoke particles, giving very early warning.
Concurrently maintainable: any component can be maintained without downtime.

q.q: An organisation plans to install liquid-cooled AI racks in an existing data hall that was designed for air-cooled servers. Which issue is MOST important to resolve before go-live?
o: Whether the hall has enough CCTV cameras to cover every one of the new racks
Whether power, cooling and floor loading can support far denser racks, with leak detection
Whether the visitor sign-in process asks every guest for photographic identification on arrival
Whether the existing fire suppression system should be replaced with halon
q.why: AI racks can draw many times the power of the servers the hall was designed for, and liquid cooling adds leak risk, so capacity, cooling, structural loading and leak detection come first. CCTV and visitor checks matter but don’t determine whether the hall can safely run the racks, and halon has long been phased out.

quiz.q: Why are ML tools such as notebooks and distributed compute dashboards frequent targets?
o: They always run on the most expensive hardware the organisation owns
They are often exposed without authentication and hold credentials and data
They can’t be patched, because their vendors never release security updates
They are used mainly by external contractors, who tend to be less careful
quiz.why: Many ML tools assume a trusted network, ship with weak or no authentication, and accumulate secrets, data and access to valuable compute.

quiz.q: Which cloud control MOST directly prevents teams creating publicly readable buckets of training data?
o: A monthly reminder email about storage good practice for all engineers
An organisation-level policy that blocks public access to storage
A naming convention that clearly marks which buckets are sensitive
Encrypting every bucket with its own customer-managed key
quiz.why: A preventive guardrail applied across the organisation stops the misconfiguration from being possible. Reminders and naming rely on people; encryption doesn’t stop public read access to decrypted objects.

quiz.q: What does a hybrid AI deployment add to hardening work?
o: Nothing, because each environment can simply be hardened on its own
Securing the links between environments, with consistent identity and policy
A requirement to move all model training back into on-premises data centres permanently
A need to switch off identity federation between the different sites
quiz.why: Hybrid adds connections and the risk of inconsistent controls, so unify identity, connect privately and apply one policy everywhere.

quiz.q: Why are plain containers a weak boundary for untrusted, agent-generated code?
o: Containers can’t limit how much memory a process is allowed to use
Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape them
Containers always have unrestricted internet access by default
Containers can only run programs written in compiled languages
quiz.why: A shared kernel means one vulnerability can break the boundary. Micro-VMs and sandboxed runtimes add a separate kernel layer.

quiz.q: Which feature is MOST characteristic of an isolated training environment for sensitive data?
o: Direct internet access, so engineers can download packages more quickly
No direct internet egress, with packages from approved internal mirrors
Shared credentials, so that any engineer can resume any training job
Public endpoints, so that research partners can submit training jobs
quiz.why: Blocking egress stops exfiltration and unreviewed downloads; dependencies come through scanned internal mirrors instead.

quiz.q: Why should prompt or key-value caches on a multi-tenant inference service be scoped per tenant?
o: Shared caches use far more memory than separate per-tenant caches would use
Shared caches can leak other tenants’ prompts through timing side channels
Per-tenant caches remove the need to authenticate requests at all
Caches can store responses in only one language at a time
quiz.why: Research in 2025 found shared prompt caches at some providers, allowing timing attacks that reveal whether others sent similar prompts.

quiz.q: Which control lets production inference keep running when experiments compete for the same GPUs?
o: A higher maximum autoscaling limit for experimental workloads
Priority classes with preemption, combined with per-team quotas
A single shared queue in which every job has equal priority
Requiring administrator approval before any experiment can run
quiz.why: Priorities with preemption guarantee capacity for production, and quotas stop any team from taking everything. Manual approval doesn’t stop runaway jobs.

quiz.q: Why should autoscaling for AI workloads have a maximum and budget alerts?
o: Autoscaling can’t add GPU nodes unless a maximum has been set
So that an attack or a bug can’t grow capacity and costs without limit
Because cloud providers forbid their customers from using unlimited autoscaling
So that experiments always receive more capacity than production
quiz.why: Unbounded autoscaling turns abuse or runaway jobs into unbounded cost. Maximums and alerts keep both in check.

quiz.q: Which way of sharing a GPU gives each workload its own memory and compute, enforced in hardware?
o: Time-slicing
Hardware partitioning
Multi-process sharing
Spot instances
quiz.why: Hardware partitioning, such as multi-instance GPU, splits a device into isolated instances with dedicated memory, cache and compute.

quiz.q: What did the 2024 LeftoverLocals research show?
o: That GPUs overheat when more than four users share them at once
That data left in GPU memory by one process could be read by another
That GPU drivers can be updated safely without rebooting servers
That time-slicing makes GPUs immune to side-channel attacks
quiz.why: Researchers recovered fragments of another process’s data, including language model output, from uncleared GPU local memory on several vendors’ devices.

quiz.q: What does 2N redundancy mean for data centre power?
o: Twice the normal number of operations staff on each shift
Fully duplicated systems and paths, either able to carry the full load
One spare component for every two that are in service
Two generators shared between all of the facility’s data halls and offices
quiz.why: 2N duplicates the entire power path, unlike N+1, which adds a single spare component.

quiz.q: Why do liquid-cooled AI racks call for leak detection?
o: Liquid cooling makes racks louder, which can drown out alarms
Coolant runs close to the electronics, so leaks can cause damage or outages
Leak sensors are needed to measure how much power the rack draws
Liquid-cooled racks have no fans, so the room’s smoke detectors stop working
quiz.why: Liquid near high-value electronics introduces a new failure mode, so leak sensors in and under racks are a standard control.

exam.q: A review of an ML platform finds a model registry with public read access, notebook servers reachable from the internet with token authentication, and GPU nodes running two-year-old drivers. What should be fixed FIRST?
o: Upgrade the GPU drivers, since outdated drivers may have known vulnerabilities
Remove public access to the registry and notebooks, and check for unauthorised use
Write a complete new hardening standard for the platform before changing anything
Rename the registry and notebook servers so that their addresses are harder to guess
exam.why: Public exposure of models and notebooks is the most immediate risk and may already have been exploited, so removing it and checking for compromise comes first. Driver updates follow quickly; standards come after the urgent fix, and obscurity isn’t a control.

exam.q: An organisation runs inference partly in its own data centre and partly in a public cloud. Audits find different firewall rules, separate identity stores and inconsistent logging. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Move everything back on premises, where the team has more direct control
Federate identity, connect privately, and apply one policy and logging standard
Accept the differences, because each environment has its own team of administrators
Ask each team to document its own rules in a shared spreadsheet for reference
exam.why: Hybrid risk comes from inconsistency. One identity system, private connectivity and a common policy and logging standard close the gaps. Retreating on premises is disproportionate, and documentation alone fixes nothing.

exam.q: A start-up’s AI service runs customer-supplied Python plugins on its inference hosts, inside the same container as the model server. Which change MOST reduces the risk?
o: Review each plugin by hand before customers are allowed to upload it
Run plugins in ephemeral micro-VM sandboxes with no network or model server access
Ask customers to sign terms promising not to upload any malicious plugins
Run the model server as root, so that it can kill any misbehaving plugins immediately
exam.why: Untrusted code needs strong isolation from the model server and the network. Manual review doesn’t scale or catch everything, terms don’t stop attackers, and running as root makes compromise worse.

exam.q: A public AI chatbot’s GPU cluster autoscaled to ten times its normal size overnight during traffic from a few hundred newly created accounts, producing a large cloud bill. Which combination BEST prevents a repeat?
o: Switch off autoscaling, so that the cluster always stays at its normal size
Per-identity token limits and quotas, an autoscaling maximum, and budget alerts
Require a credit card for every new account, and take no other action
Move the chatbot to a cloud provider that charges less for GPU time
exam.why: Per-identity limits stop a few accounts consuming capacity, the maximum caps scale, and alerts catch anomalies early. Disabling autoscaling hurts legitimate peaks, and payment checks or cheaper GPUs don’t limit consumption.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud-scoring model must respond within 50 milliseconds around the clock. It runs on spot GPU instances shared with batch analytics. What is the BEST change?
o: Keep the spot instances but add more of them, so that reclaim events matter less
Move it to reserved, dedicated capacity across zones, with a fallback model
Time-slice the GPUs more aggressively, so that the model gets more turns
Run the model on analysts’ laptops whenever there is a GPU shortage
exam.why: Critical, latency-sensitive services need capacity that can’t be reclaimed or crowded out, spread for resilience, with a fallback. More spot instances still share the reclaim risk, and time-slicing adds unpredictability.

exam.q: A colocation provider hosting a company’s AI training hardware proposes removing the mantrap at the data hall entrance and relying on badge access alone. What should the company’s security lead do?
o: Accept the change, because the badge readers already record who enters the hall
Object: layered entry controls stop tailgating to high-value hardware; check the contract
Accept, provided the provider adds a sign reminding staff not to hold the doors open for others
Object, but only because removing it might affect the fire suppression system
exam.why: Badges record a card, not the people who follow it in. A mantrap prevents tailgating to high-value hardware, and the contract and audit reports should require it. Signs aren’t controls, and fire suppression isn’t the issue.

exam.q: The facilities team proposes gaseous fire suppression throughout a new AI data hall, including an area where technicians routinely work. What is the MAIN additional consideration?
o: Gaseous systems leave a residue that damages GPUs and network equipment
People safety: alarms, discharge delays, evacuation procedures and room sealing
Gaseous systems can’t be combined with any form of early smoke detection
Gaseous suppression is prohibited in every building that uses liquid cooling
exam.why: Gas systems are effective and leave no residue, but occupied spaces need pre-discharge alarms, delays, evacuation and safety procedures, and rooms must be sealed for the agent to work. They are commonly paired with early detection.
